title: Longest streak of days
statement:
A habit tracker stores the day numbers on which you practiced, in no particular order and possibly with repeats.

Return the length of the longest streak: the longest run of consecutive day numbers that all appear in `days`. Your solution should run in linear time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can days repeat?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A repeated day counts once in a streak.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Duplicates break approaches that count array positions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can day numbers be negative or zero?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Rules out using day numbers as array indexes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the list is empty?
Is sorting allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It works, but aim for linear time.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Tells you the n log n solution is the baseline, not the goal.

edgeCases.why: Duplicates must not inflate or split the streak.

approaches.name: Check each number by stepping up
approaches.idea: For each number, count how many of number + 1, + 2, ... are in the list, scanning the list each time.

approaches.name: Sort then scan
approaches.idea: Sort, skip duplicates, and count runs where each value is one more than the previous.
approaches.space: O(n) or O(1) depending on the sort
approaches.tradeoffs: Simple and good in practice, but not linear.

approaches.name: Hash set, start only at streak beginnings
approaches.idea: Put all days in a set. Only start counting from a day whose previous day is missing, then step up while the next day is present.
approaches.tradeoffs: Each day is visited a constant number of times overall, because counting starts only at the beginning of a streak.

optimal.name: Hash set with streak starts
optimal.explanation: Build a set of the days. For each day d in the set where d - 1 is not in the set, count up from d while d + length is in the set and keep the maximum. Because counting only starts at streak beginnings, the total work across all streaks is O(n).

hintLadder: Sorting would work. What does it cost, and is there a faster way to ask whether a number is present?
If you can check membership in constant time, how would you measure a streak starting at some day?
You would repeat a lot of work if you counted from every day. Which days are worth starting from?
Only start counting from a day whose previous day is not in the set.

expectedMentions.what: Mentions the sort-based O(n log n) solution
Proposes a hash set for constant-time lookups and O(n) total time
Explains why counting only from streak starts keeps the total linear
Notes the O(n) extra space for the set
Traces an example with duplicates or an unordered streak

followUps: Days arrive one at a time; report the longest streak after each arrival.

walkthrough.say: Can the same day appear twice? And can day numbers be negative? If the list is empty I’ll return zero.
The easy baseline is sorting, then walking through and counting runs, skipping duplicates. That’s n log n. You mentioned linear time, so let me think about avoiding the sort.
If I put every day in a hash set, I can ask whether any day is present in constant time. From a day d, I can count d plus one, d plus two, and so on.

But if I count from every day, a long streak gets recounted from each of its days, which is quadratic. The fix is to only start counting at the first day of a streak, where d minus one isn’t in the set. Then each day is stepped over once. That’s O(n) time and O(n) space.
Build the set first, then loop over the set, not the list, so duplicates don’t repeat work.
This is a streak start. Step up while the next day exists.
walkthrough.code:
length = 1
            while d + length in present:

            best = max(best, length)
    return best

walkthrough.say: For 12, 4, 11, 1, 10, 3, 2: 1 has no 0, so I count 1, 2, 3, 4, length 4. 10 has no 9, so 10, 11, 12, length 3. The others have a predecessor and are skipped. Answer 4.
With 5, 5, 6, 6, 7 the set is 5, 6, 7, so I get 3, and an empty list never enters the loop and returns 0.
Linear time and linear space. The sorted version uses less memory if I can sort in place, so that’s the tradeoff.
